title: The CD Rollover Trap: Your Renewal Rate Is Not the Market Rate
description: Reg DD lets the pre-maturity notice arrive with the renewal rate blank, and the grace period that follows can be five days long. What the bank must send, and what it does not.
content:
The certificate matures on a Thursday. The envelope arrived three weeks earlier and ran to a single page: the maturity date, a line saying the account renews for another twelve months, and, in the space where the new rate should have been, a sentence explaining that the rate has not been set yet, followed by a date and a telephone number. A new twelve-month CD at the same bank, tagged for new deposits, can advertise a rate well above what the renewal will pay.

No rule is being broken and nothing is hidden. Federal deposit rules decide what a bank has to tell a depositor and when it has to say it. They do not decide what it pays. Regulation DD states its own ambition at [12 CFR 1030.1(b)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/section-1030.1): "The purpose of this part is to enable consumers to make informed decisions about accounts at depository institutions. This part requires depository institutions to provide disclosures so that consumers can make meaningful comparisons among depository institutions." Comparison is the whole of the remedy. Nothing in the rule requires the renewal rate to match the rate the same bank is advertising further down the page.

The [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/) says as much in plainer words on its consumer page about [CD rollovers](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-certificate-of-deposit-cd-rollover-or-renewal-en-923/): "The interest rate for the new CD is not guaranteed to be the same as the interest rate for your current CD." Higher or lower, and the depositor finds out by asking.

What the rules do supply is a deadline and a door. The deadline is a pre-maturity notice with a fixed mailing date. The door is the grace period, defined at [12 CFR 1030.2(m)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1030/2/) as "a period following the maturity of an automatically renewing time account during which the consumer may withdraw funds without being assessed a penalty." Whether that door exists at all, and how wide it opens, is the bank's choice, subject to disclosure. The bank need not pay interest for the days the money sits inside it. Once it shuts, the deposit is committed to a term it was never priced for, with an early withdrawal penalty as the only exit.

## The notice that has to arrive before maturity

The timing rule is in [12 CFR 1030.5(b)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1030/5/), and it covers only part of the CD universe: "For time accounts with a maturity longer than one month that renew automatically at maturity, institutions shall provide the disclosures described below before maturity." Two mailing deadlines follow, and the bank picks one.

The default runs from maturity. "The disclosures shall be mailed or delivered at least 30 calendar days before maturity of the existing account." The alternative is tied to the grace period: "the disclosures may be mailed or delivered at least 20 calendar days before the end of the grace period on the existing account, provided a grace period of at least five calendar days is allowed."

The second option trades a shorter warning for a longer window. Its clock runs backward from the end of the grace period rather than from maturity, so a longer grace period buys the bank a later mailing. The [official interpretations](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1030/Interp-5/) work one case: "Under the alternative timing rule, an institution offering a 10-day grace period would have to provide the disclosures at least 10 days prior to the scheduled maturity date." The same subtraction fills in the rest:

| Grace period offered | Notice due under the alternative rule |
|---|---|
| 5 calendar days | 15 days before maturity |
| 10 calendar days | 10 days before maturity |
| 15 calendar days | 5 days before maturity |
| 20 calendar days | the maturity date itself |

A depositor who assumes the envelope always comes a month early is assuming the default. Under the alternative, notice a week before maturity is compliant, and behind a long grace period it can land on the day the CD comes due.

What the notice must contain splits by term. For maturities longer than one year, 1030.5(b)(1) requires "account disclosures set forth in § 1030.4(b) of this part for the new account, along with the date the existing account matures," which means the whole opening package: rate, compounding, fees, the early withdrawal penalty, the renewal policy. At one year or less but longer than one month, 1030.5(b)(2) permits a far shorter notice instead, limited to three items. "The date the existing account matures and the new maturity date if the account is renewed." The rate and annual percentage yield "if they are known." And "any difference in the terms of the new account as compared to the terms required to be disclosed under § 1030.4(b) of this part for the existing account."

Any certificate of twelve months or less sits in that bracket, so the renewal notice on a one-year CD can run to three lines. It is not required to restate the penalty, the compounding method, or anything else that has not changed.

Delivery is governed by [12 CFR 1030.3(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/section-1030.3), which allows electronic form "subject to compliance with the consumer consent and other applicable provisions of the Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act." For an account opened online, the notice that starts the clock may be a message in a portal, and it satisfies the rule whether or not anyone signs in to read it.

One category gets no notice at all. Section 1030.5(c) covers non-renewing accounts, but only long ones: "For time accounts with a maturity longer than one year that do not renew automatically at maturity, institutions shall disclose to consumers the maturity date and whether interest will be paid after maturity," at least ten calendar days ahead. A six-month CD that does not renew falls outside both 1030.5(b) and 1030.5(c). Nothing has to be mailed, and the commentary on 1030.7(a)(1) confirms the earnings can stop: institutions "are not required to pay interest after time accounts mature," including "following the maturity of nonrollover time accounts." Other terms buried in the same opening package are catalogued in [Six Lines in a Bank Disclosure That Decide What You Earn](/2026/08/24/six-lines-in-a-bank-disclosure-that-decide-what-you-earn/).

## The rate the notice is allowed to leave blank

Both versions of the notice share one escape hatch, and the rule spells it out. From 1030.5(b)(1): "If the interest rate and annual percentage yield that will be paid for the new account are unknown when disclosures are provided, the institution shall state that those rates have not yet been determined, the date when they will be determined, and a telephone number consumers may call to obtain the interest rate and the annual percentage yield that will be paid for the new account."

[Appendix B to Part 1030](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/appendix-Appendix%20B%20to%20Part%201030) prints the sentence banks use. Model Clause B-3(a), for automatically renewable accounts of one year or less but longer than one month, offers the rate line in two forms: "The interest rate for the renewed account will be ____% with an annual percentage yield of ____%," or, failing that, "The interest rate and annual percentage yield have not yet been determined. They will be available on (date). Please call (phone number) to learn the interest rate and annual percentage yield for your new account."

The commentary is relaxed about how precisely that date gets pinned down. Acceptable answers include "a specific date, such as 'October 28,'" or "a date that is easily determinable, such as 'the Tuesday before the maturity date stated on this notice' or 'as of the maturity date stated on this notice.'" That last option lets the notice promise the renewal rate on the maturity date, the day the renewal happens.

That leaves the phone call, which has a rule of its own. Under [12 CFR 1030.3(e)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/section-1030.3), "in an oral response to a consumer's inquiry about interest rates payable on its accounts, the depository institution shall state the annual percentage yield. The interest rate may be stated in addition to the annual percentage yield. No other rate may be stated." A figure quoted over the phone is an APY unless the representative separately labels an interest rate, which makes it directly comparable to any other APY. Nothing else, including a promotional rate on some unrelated product, is a permitted answer to the question.

Written quotes carry a documented looseness. Section 1030.4(a)(2)(ii)(A) lets an institution responding to a request "specify an interest rate and annual percentage yield that were offered within the most recent seven calendar days; state that the rate and yield are accurate as of an identified date; and provide a telephone number consumers may call to obtain current rate information." A rate sheet handed across a counter can be a week stale by permission.

## Grace period mechanics

The grace period is a creature of contract that federal rules describe rather than require. Section 1030.4(b)(6)(iv), the renewal policies item in the opening disclosures, demands "a statement of whether or not the account will renew automatically at maturity. If it will, a statement of whether or not a grace period will be provided and, if so, the length of that period must be stated." The model clauses in Appendix B, at B-1(h)(iv), give both answers: "You will have [____ calendar/business] days after the maturity date to withdraw funds without penalty," or "There is no grace period following the maturity of this account to withdraw funds without penalty."

The second clause exists because the second outcome is allowed. A CD can renew with no window at all, and a disclosure saying so is compliant.

The common ten-day figure traces back to a footnote in the Federal Reserve's Regulation D. [12 CFR 204.2](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/section-204.2) defines a time deposit around a mandatory penalty of "at least seven days' simple interest on amounts withdrawn within the first six days after deposit," and footnote 1 lists the cases where an institution may pay out early without imposing it. Item (f) on that list: "Where a time deposit is withdrawn within ten days after a specified maturity date even though the deposit contract provided for automatic renewal at the maturity date."

That clears the federal obstacle to a ten-day exit from a freshly renewed term. It does not create a right to one. The depositor's window is whatever the account disclosure states, and the regulation's only contribution is to make the longer choices possible.

Two other items on the same list have nothing to do with rate shopping. A deposit may be paid without penalty "upon the death of any owner of the time deposit funds." The same goes for the portion of a deposit that lost federal insurance when two insured banks merged, "for a period of one year from the date of the merger." The deposit insurance side of that scenario is in [When Your Bank Is Acquired, Not Failed: What Happens to Your CD](/2026/09/03/when-your-bank-is-acquired-not-failed-what-happens-to-your-cd/).

Credit unions run on a parallel track. Regulation DD "applies to depository institutions except for credit unions" under 1030.1(c), and share certificates follow the National Credit Union Administration's Truth in Savings rule at [12 CFR 707.5](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/section-707.5), which repeats the structure almost word for word with "term share account" in place of time account and "dividend rate" in place of interest rate. The thirty days, the twenty-day alternative and the five-day floor on the grace period all carry over.

## Interest during the days between two terms

The grace period suspends the penalty. It does not guarantee earnings. Comment 5 to 1030.7(a)(1) in the [official interpretations](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1030/Interp-7/) says so directly: "Institutions are not required to pay interest after time accounts mature." The first example given is this exact situation, "during a grace period offered for an automatically renewable time account, if consumers decide during that period not to renew the account."

The disclosure rules do not close the gap either. The interpretation of the renewal policies item states that institutions "offering a grace period on time accounts that automatically renew need not state whether interest will be paid if the funds are withdrawn during the grace period." A bank is free to pay the new term's rate for those days, to pay nothing, or to say nothing about which it does.

On $25,000 moving to a replacement paying 4%, eight unpaid days come to $21.92 of interest that exists in neither account. Against a rate gap measured in hundreds of dollars that is a rounding error. It turns into something larger when the window is treated as a free look: every day left inside a renewed CD paying almost nothing costs the difference.

Confirm the numbers before moving, in this order: the renewal APY, the length of the grace period, and whether interest accrues inside it.

## The cost of noticing late

Miss the window and the money sits inside a new term at the new rate, with the old exit price attached. The penalty is disclosed under 1030.4(b)(6)(ii), which requires "a statement that a penalty will or may be imposed for early withdrawal, how it is calculated, and the conditions for its assessment." Because it is usually written in days of interest, it is computed on the renewed balance at the renewed rate, which shrinks the penalty as the rate falls.

Take $25,000 in a twelve-month CD that renews at 1% when a competitive alternative pays 4%, with a 180-day penalty. Daily interest on the renewed CD is $25,000 × 1% ÷ 365 = $0.6849, so the penalty is $123.29 whenever it is triggered. What moves is the prize:

| When the depositor acts | Extra interest at 4% over the remaining term | Penalty | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inside the grace period | $750.00 | none | +$750.00 |
| Day 30 of the new term | $688.36 | $123.29 | +$565.07 |
| Day 180 | $380.14 | $123.29 | +$256.85 |
| Day 300 | $133.56 | $123.29 | +$10.27 |
| Day 330 | $71.92 | $123.29 | −$51.37 |

Acting inside the grace period is worth roughly $185 more than acting a month later, which is the real price of an envelope that went unopened. A late exit still usually beats no exit: at day 180 the switch clears $256.85 after the penalty. The point where waiting wins arrives late: the extra interest stops covering the $123.29 penalty once roughly 60 days are left.

The low renewal rate is what makes the penalty survivable. Had the CD renewed at 4% and the alternative paid 7%, the same 180-day penalty would come to $493.15, four times larger, because the penalty is denominated in the account's own interest. Cheap CDs are cheap to leave. The general version of this calculation, including partial withdrawals, is in [When Breaking a CD Actually Pays: Run the Break-Even](/2026/08/25/when-breaking-a-cd-actually-pays-run-the-break-even/), and what the penalty is worth on the tax return is in [CD Early Withdrawal Penalties: The Disclosure and the Deduction](/2026/09/22/cd-early-withdrawal-penalties-the-disclosure-and-the-deduction/).

A ladder removes the deadline problem instead of managing it. A maturity lands on the calendar every few months, so the renewal decision becomes a recurring appointment rather than an annual ambush. The arithmetic of building one while short terms pay best is in [Building a CD Ladder When 12-Month CDs Pay the Most](/2026/08/19/building-a-cd-ladder-when-12-month-cds-pay-the-most/).

## Benchmarks for the renewal rate

The free public benchmark is the [FDIC](https://www.fdic.gov/national-rates-and-rate-caps)'s national rate table, which as of August 17, 2026 put the twelve-month CD national average at 1.71% and the sixty-month average at 1.36%, with savings accounts at 0.38%. Against numbers like those a renewal quote lands as above or below the middle of the market.

The FDIC's own page attaches three caveats to that comparison.

The figure is a deposit-weighted average, defined as "the average of rates paid by all insured depository institutions and credit unions for which data is available, with rates weighted by each institution's share of domestic deposits." Institutions holding the most money count the most, which pulls the average toward the largest branch networks rather than toward the best available offer. Beating the average is a low bar, not a target.

The tiers matter too. CD figures "represent an average of the $10,000 and $100,000 product tiers," so a small certificate is being held up against pricing set for larger ones.

And the number is old before it posts. The table "will be published every 3rd Monday of each month," while the inputs are "based on information available on the last business day of the prior month end." What appears on screen can be three weeks behind the market, which matters most when rates move quickly. Why posted rates lag harder in one direction than the other is covered in [Why Your Savings Rate Drops Faster Than It Rises](/2026/09/01/deposit-betas-why-savings-rates-fall-faster-than-they-rise/).

The same page carries a second figure that is not a consumer rate at all. The national rate cap, listed at 5.65% for twelve-month CDs on the August 17, 2026 table, is a supervisory ceiling. It is "calculated as the higher of: (1) the national rate plus 75 basis points; or (2) 120 percent of the current yield on similar maturity U.S. Department of the Treasury obligations plus 75 basis points," and it limits what a less than well capitalized institution may offer. It is neither a forecast nor an average, and no one is promising to pay it.

For a like-for-like check on the term itself, Treasury yields published by the government cover the same maturities, and the tax treatment differs enough to reorder the ranking. That comparison is worked through in [Treasury Bills vs CDs: The Tax Break That Changes the Comparison](/2026/09/23/treasury-bills-vs-cds-the-tax-break-that-changes-the-comparison/).

## What else can change at renewal

The rate is the visible term. It is not the only one that resets.

Under 1030.5(b)(2)(ii)(C), the short notice has to flag "any difference in the terms of the new account as compared to the terms required to be disclosed under § 1030.4(b) of this part for the existing account." That list takes in the early withdrawal penalty, the compounding and crediting schedule, minimum balance requirements, and fees. A renewal can carry a longer penalty than the term that just ended, and the differences line is the only place it appears.

The commentary separates two kinds of change at rollover. If the institution initiates it, the pre-maturity notice rules apply. If the consumer initiates it, "the account opening disclosure requirements of § 1030.4(b) apply," and the worked example is a depositor who receives a notice on a one-year CD and asks to roll into a six-month one: the institution "must provide either account opening disclosures including the new maturity date or, if all other terms previously disclosed in the prematurity notice remain the same, only the new maturity date."

Mid-term changes are handled elsewhere. Section 1030.5(a)(1) requires 30 calendar days' advance notice "of any change in a term required to be disclosed under § 1030.4(b) of this part if the change may reduce the annual percentage yield or adversely affect the consumer." One exception covers the shortest CDs, at 1030.5(a)(2)(iii): no notice for "changes in any term for time accounts with maturities of one month or less." A 28-day CD on automatic renewal sits outside both the change-in-terms notice and the pre-maturity notice, since 1030.5(b) starts above one month. It can reprice indefinitely in silence.

Deposit insurance can turn on a renewal as well. [12 CFR 330.4(b)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/section-330.4) continues separate coverage for six months after one insured institution assumes another's deposits, then adds a rule specific to CDs: time deposits maturing inside that window "and which are renewed at the same dollar amount (either with or without accrued interest having been added to the principal amount) and for the same term as the original deposit" stay separately insured "until the first maturity date after the six-month period." Those "renewed on any other basis, or that are not renewed and thereby become demand deposits, are separately insured only until the end of the six-month period." Changing the term or the amount at renewal, which is the ordinary response to a bad rate, is what ends the extra coverage.

Interest earned in the old term is taxed whether or not it leaves the bank. [IRS Publication 550](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550) sets the general standard: "You constructively receive income when it is credited to your account or made available to you. You do not need to have physical possession of it." It is blunter about renewals in its discussion of original issue discount: "Renewable certificates. If you renew a CD at maturity, it is treated as a redemption and a purchase of a new certificate. This is true regardless of the terms of renewal." Rolling interest into the next term defers nothing. Why a long CD can produce a tax bill years before the money is reachable is in [Why You Owe Tax on a 5-Year CD You Cannot Touch Yet](/2026/09/25/why-you-owe-tax-on-a-5-year-cd-you-cannot-touch-yet/).

Set the renewal quote beside the outside offer below, at the same balance and the same term, while the grace period is still open.

{% include tools/two-offer-comparison.html %}

## Common questions

**Does the bank have to tell me the renewal rate before the CD renews?** Not necessarily. Section 1030.5(b)(1) permits a notice stating that "those rates have not yet been determined, the date when they will be determined, and a telephone number consumers may call," and the commentary accepts a determination date as late as "the maturity date stated on this notice." The obligation is to give a way to find out, not to quote a number in advance.

**What happens if the grace period closes before I act?** The deposit is committed to the new term at the new rate, and withdrawing triggers the early withdrawal penalty disclosed under 1030.4(b)(6)(ii). Because most penalties are expressed in days of interest on the account's own rate, a penalty calculated on a low renewal rate is small in dollars, and the break-even frequently still favors moving.

**Is a grace period required by law?** No. Section 1030.4(b)(6)(iv) requires the bank to state whether one is provided and how long it runs, and Appendix B supplies a model clause for accounts that offer none. Regulation D's footnote 1(f) permits, without requiring, a penalty-free withdrawal "within ten days after a specified maturity date" on a contract that renews automatically.

**Does the money earn interest during the grace period?** The commentary says interest is not required after maturity, and the disclosure rules add that a bank offering a grace period "need not state whether interest will be paid if the funds are withdrawn during the grace period." It is a question for the institution, and the answer is not standard across banks.

**Can a renewal change the penalty or the fees, not just the rate?** Yes. For maturities of one year or less, 1030.5(b)(2)(ii)(C) requires the notice to disclose "any difference in the terms of the new account" measured against the 1030.4(b) disclosures for the old one. Above a year, 1030.5(b)(1) requires the full set of account disclosures for the new account, penalty included.

The bank picks the mailing schedule, the rate inside the notice may be blank by design, and the window it announces can be five days long. The one date in the sequence that does not depend on an envelope is the maturity printed on the opening disclosure.

title: You Wired It Yourself: Why Regulation E Will Not Get That Money Back
description: Regulation E covers a transfer initiated by someone other than you. Where the scammer talks you into sending it, the claim fails on the first element, and the recovery clock moves to the FBI.
content:
The call came in at 2:40 on a Tuesday afternoon, and the number on the screen matched the one printed on the back of the debit card. The man gave a badge number, said accounts had been opened that morning in three states, and said the only way to stop the next withdrawal was to move the balance into a holding account. He read out a routing number twice and waited while it was written down. The wire left at 3:15 p.m. for $18,400, the entire savings balance. At the branch the next morning, the manager pulled the record, looked up, and said the transfer was authorized.

That answer is correct in the only sense the governing rule cares about. Federal protection for electronic transfers out of a consumer account turns on six words buried in one definition: a person other than the consumer. [12 CFR 1005.2(m)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/2/) defines an unauthorized electronic fund transfer as one "initiated by a person other than the consumer without actual authority to initiate the transfer and from which the consumer receives no benefit." A transfer the consumer typed, confirmed, and sent fails that first element before any question of deception arises.

There is a version of the same afternoon that ends differently. If the caller had talked the account holder into reading out a login and a texted confirmation code, and had then moved the money himself, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's own compliance guidance says the result is an unauthorized transfer with full liability protection. Nothing about the lie changes between the two versions. What changes is whose hands were on the keyboard when the money moved.

The line between a covered claim and a denied one is drawn by who pressed send, not by how convincing the story was. A recall is a request the receiving institution is free to refuse. And the machinery that can freeze the funds sits at the FBI and the Treasury Department rather than at the bank, runs on a clock measured in hours, and has to be started by the person who sent the money.

## The six words that decide the claim

Regulation E, which implements the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, carries its entire fraud allocation in the definition at 1005.2(m). The positive test requires a transfer "initiated by a person other than the consumer," made "without actual authority," and "from which the consumer receives no benefit." The elements are cumulative, which is why the third is no help here: a transfer that fails the first never reaches it.

Three carve-outs follow, excluding a transfer initiated:

1. "By a person who was furnished the access device to the consumer's account by the consumer, unless the consumer has notified the financial institution that transfers by that person are no longer authorized."
2. "With fraudulent intent by the consumer or any person acting in concert with the consumer."
3. "By the financial institution or its employee."

The [official interpretations](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/Interp-2/) work the edges, and two of the five comments do most of the work. Comment 2(m)-3 reads: "an unauthorized EFT includes a transfer initiated by a person who obtained the access device from the consumer through fraud or robbery." Under Comment 2(m)-4, "an EFT at an ATM is an unauthorized transfer if the consumer has been induced by force to initiate the transfer."

Comment 4 is the one place in the commentary where a consumer's own hands on the terminal still produce an unauthorized transfer, and the trigger there is force, not persuasion. A person marched to an ATM at knifepoint is covered. A person talked into a wire by a stranger claiming to be from the fraud department is not addressed at all, because the drafters treated a transfer the consumer chose to make as the consumer's transfer.

Comment 2(m)-2 handles the case that looks closest to a scam and is treated furthest from one: a consumer who furnishes an access device to someone "who exceeds the authority given" is "fully liable for the transfers" until the institution is told that person is no longer authorized. Handing the card and PIN to a relative who then takes more than agreed is a dispute between two people, one of whom has the money.

## Credentials taken, or a payment sent

The Bureau's [Electronic Fund Transfers FAQs](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/compliance-resources/deposit-accounts-resources/electronic-fund-transfers/electronic-fund-transfers-faqs/), a compliance aid at Version 3 and last updated January 15, 2025, spends a full section on unauthorized transfers.

Question 5 asks whether the definition is met when "a third party fraudulently induces a consumer into sharing account access information that is used to initiate an EFT from the consumer's account." The answer is yes. One of the Bureau's examples is "a third-party calling the consumer and pretending to be a representative from the consumer's financial institution and then tricking the consumer into providing their account login information, texted account confirmation code, debit card number, or other information that could be used to initiate an EFT out of the consumer's account."

Question 6 closes the escape route institutions reach for first. Asked whether transfers made with fraudulently obtained credentials fall inside the first carve-out because the consumer handed the information over, the Bureau answers no: "A consumer who is fraudulently induced into providing account information has not furnished an access device under Regulation E."

The rest of the section removes the usual defenses. Question 7 says an institution may not weigh the consumer's carelessness, quoting Comment 6(b)-2 that writing a PIN on the card "does not affect the consumer's liability for unauthorized transfers under Regulation E." Question 8 forecloses contracting around any of it, citing the anti-waiver provision at 15 U.S.C. 1693l. Nor can network rules do that work. Under Question 10, finality and irrevocability between banks "do not reduce consumer protections against liability for unauthorized EFTs afforded by the Electronic Fund Transfer Act."

That is a strong set of protections, and every one describes the same fact pattern. In Question 4's examples a hacker breaks into a merchant's systems, a fraudster hacks a phone and uses the mobile wallet, a thief steals a wallet; in Question 5 the third party takes the login and uses it. The fraudster initiates. The section contains no question in which the consumer opens the app, enters an amount, and taps send, because that transaction is not an unauthorized transfer.

## The payments the rule never reached

For a wire, the threshold question is not liability but coverage. [12 CFR 1005.3(c)(3)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/3/) excludes from coverage "any transfer of funds through Fedwire or through a similar wire transfer system that is used primarily for transfers between financial institutions or between businesses." The [commentary](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/interp-3/) names the similar systems: "the Clearing House Interbank Payments System (CHIPS), Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT), Telex, and transfers made on the books of correspondent banks."

A retail wire from a checking account runs on those rails, and the exclusion does not turn on who initiated it. The commentary points instead to state law, citing UCC section 4A-202 for a telephone-initiated Fedwire payment. [UCC 4A-108](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/4A/4A-108) states the division from the other side: "this Article does not apply to a funds transfer any part of which is governed by the Electronic Fund Transfer Act of 1978." For a consumer wire, then, the governing law is Article 4A, a commercial code written for banks and businesses rather than a consumer protection statute.

One carve-in matters. Subpart B covers remittance transfers to recipients abroad, with [1005.30(e)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/30/) excluding transfers of "$15 or less" and 1005.30(f) providing a safe harbor to a person that both provided and provides "500 or fewer remittance transfers" in the previous and the current calendar year. What it adds is a clock most senders never hear about. [12 CFR 1005.34](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/34/) requires a provider to honor a cancellation request received "no later than 30 minutes after the sender makes payment," so long as it identifies the sender and the particular transfer and "the transferred funds have not been picked up by the designated recipient or deposited into an account of the designated recipient." The refund then covers the total amount provided, fees and taxes included, within three business days. Thirty minutes is short and that second condition is the one that usually fails, but for a transfer where doubt sets in on the walk back to the car, the deadline is worth knowing.

Whether the institution behind an app-based transfer is even a bank is a separate question worth settling first, and the answer is not always what the marketing implies, as [When FDIC Insured Means a Partner Bank, Not Your App](/2026/09/08/when-fdic-insured-means-a-partner-bank-not-your-app/) works through.

## What a recall request can and cannot do

The word the branch will use is recall, and it sounds like a reversal. Article 4A defines it narrowly. [UCC 4A-211](https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/4A/4A-211) lets a sender cancel a payment order "orally, electronically, or in writing," effective under subsection (b) only if it arrives in time for the receiving bank "to act on the communication before the bank accepts the payment order." That window closes in the minutes before acceptance, not the hours after a scam is discovered.

Subsection (c) then decides most cases: "After a payment order has been accepted, cancellation or amendment of the order is not effective unless the receiving bank agrees or a funds-transfer system rule allows cancellation or amendment without agreement of the bank." Once the beneficiary's bank has accepted, the sending bank has no power to claw the payment back. It can ask. The receiving institution decides, weighing its own exposure to a customer whose account it would be debiting.

Hence the indemnity attached to the recall paperwork. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center states the first move in its published [domestic kill chain process](https://www.justice.gov/elderjustice/media/1364051/dl?inline=): "Contact the originating Financial Institution as soon as fraud is recognized to request a recall or reversal as well as a Hold Harmless Letter or Letter of Indemnity."

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency sets the ceiling on expectations. Asked whether a customer can be held liable after wiring money to a scammer, [HelpWithMyBank.gov](https://www.helpwithmybank.gov/help-topics/fraud-scams/scams/wire-transfer-scams/wire-transfer-scams-held-liable.html) answers: "Your bank would need to review your fraud claim. Wire transfers are intended to be a final and irrevocable method of payment and the bank may not be able to reverse the wire transfer." Its page on what to do about a fraudulent wire adds the instruction easiest to miss, which is to call both ends: "Contact your bank and the bank that may have received your funds."

The ACH side is narrower still. Nacha's rules permit a reversing entry only to correct an erroneous entry, and [Nacha's own summary](https://www.nacha.org/news/second-chance-understanding-ach-reversals) lists what qualifies: a "duplicate payment, incorrect amount, payment sent on the wrong date, or payment sent to an unintended account," transmitted "within five banking days of the original settlement date." A payment the sender meant to send, in the amount intended, to the account number written on a receipt, is not on that list. What the bank sends instead is a request, answered at the receiving institution's discretion.

Underneath all of it sits a timing problem no letter solves. Accounts opened to receive scam proceeds do not hold the money long, which is the premise both federal programs are built on. It is also why receiving institutions close them, and why the people who opened them often cannot open another, a consequence covered in [Denied a Bank Account Because of ChexSystems: What to Do](/2026/09/16/denied-a-bank-account-because-of-chexsystems-what-to-do/). By the time a recall request is drafted, the question is usually not whether the receiving bank will agree but whether anything is left to agree about.

## The first seventy-two hours

Two federal programs aim at this gap.

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network's [Rapid Response Program](https://www.fincen.gov/system/files/shared/RRP%20Fact%20Sheet%20Notice%20FINAL%20508.pdf), described in a fact sheet issued February 11, 2022, states the finding directly: "the RRP has had greater success in recovering funds when victims or financial institutions report fraudulently induced wire transfers to law enforcement within 72 hours of the transaction." The fact sheet puts the cumulative result at "more than $1.1 billion" recovered for U.S. victims since 2015, working through counterpart financial intelligence units abroad.

The activation path is specific: "A victim of a cyber-enabled crime, or the victim's financial institution, must file a complaint with law enforcement to initiate the RRP," through the FBI's complaint center or the nearest Secret Service field office, and "Victims should not directly contact FinCEN." The required fields are worth writing down before calling, because a complaint missing any of them stalls:

- Victim's name, the victim's financial institution's name, and the country location of the originating branch
- The victim's account name, which the fact sheet notes "may be different than the victim's name," and account number
- The beneficiary's financial institution's name and the country location of the receiving branch
- The beneficiary's account name and account number
- Date of the wire transaction, and the currency and amount transferred

The fact sheet closes that list with one line: "Time is of the essence to successfully recover funds!"

The domestic counterpart is the Recovery Asset Team at the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center, established in February 2018, which runs the Financial Fraud Kill Chain. The [2025 IC3 Annual Report](https://www.ic3.gov/AnnualReport/Reports/2025_IC3Report.pdf) gives the year's totals: 3,900 incidents, $1,163,919,846 in attempted theft, $679,013,183 frozen, a 58% success rate. It notes a shift away from business email compromise toward tech support and account takeover cases, the latter sometimes involving "50 or more transactions to different recipient accounts at multiple banks happening simultaneously via ACH transactions."

Its guidance to victims repeats both halves of the sequence: "If you discover a fraudulent transfer, time is of the essence. Immediately, contact your financial institution and request a recall of the funds along with any necessary indemnification documents." Then: "Regardless of the amount lost, file a complaint at www.ic3.gov." That second instruction is unconditional, and the report's note that "different financial institutions have varying policies" warns that the first step may produce nothing.

Against $20.877 billion in total reported losses for 2025, a 58% freeze rate on the cases that reach the team in time is the best number in this subject, and the one that decays fastest with delay.

## Where each report actually lands

The reports people are told to file after a scam do different jobs.

A complaint at ic3.gov is the one with a recovery mechanism bolted to it. It triggers the Recovery Asset Team and is the route the FinCEN fact sheet names for reaching the international program. Transaction detail is not a formality; the freeze request sent to the recipient bank is built from the account numbers in the complaint.

[ReportFraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov/) feeds the Federal Trade Commission's enforcement and data work. The agency's guidance on [what to do if you were scammed](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-do-if-you-were-scammed) is organized by payment method and, in every case, points first at the company that moved the money rather than at itself: report a wire "to the wire transfer company immediately," a payment app payment "to the payment app immediately." That ordering describes where the leverage sits.

The [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's complaint process](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/complaint/process/) is a routing service with a clock. The Bureau forwards it to the company, and "companies generally respond in 15 days," with some taking up to 60. It does not adjudicate, but it does put a written answer on the record from an institution that may otherwise have given only a verbal denial at a counter.

Which prudential regulator hears a complaint depends on the charter: national banks and federal savings associations answer to the OCC through HelpWithMyBank.gov, federal credit unions to the National Credit Union Administration, state-chartered institutions to a state regulator and often to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation or the Federal Reserve. Working out which applies is the lookup described in [How to Verify a Bank Is Actually FDIC Insured Before You Transfer](/2026/09/09/how-to-verify-a-bank-is-actually-fdic-insured-before-you-transfer/), run in reverse. A local police report belongs on the list for an unrelated reason: insurers, employers, and adult protective services routinely ask for a report number, and it is easier to get in week one than in month three.

None of these returns money on its own. One of them can freeze it.

## The error resolution that still applies

A denial under 1005.2(m) does not empty the file. [12 CFR 1005.11](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/11/) defines an "error" as a list of seven items. The first is "an unauthorized electronic fund transfer." The seventh is "the consumer's request for documentation required by § 1005.9 or § 1005.10(a) or for additional information or clarification concerning an electronic fund transfer."

That seventh item is available whether or not the first is. A written request for the transfer record, the timestamps, the channel the instruction arrived through, and the institution's own findings is itself a notice of error, and it starts the same clocks: 10 business days to investigate and three more to report, extendable to 45 days if the account is provisionally credited within the 10. The outer limit stretches to 90 days for a transfer that was not initiated within a state, a point-of-sale debit card transaction, or one that occurred within 30 days after the first deposit to the account.

Section 1005.11(d) governs the denial itself. The institution must give "a written explanation of the institution's findings" and tell the consumer of the right to request the documents it relied on. A verbal no at a counter does not satisfy that, and those documents are the only way to test whether the institution determined who initiated the transfer or simply assumed it. Under [15 U.S.C. 1693f(e)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1693f), the consumer is entitled to treble damages where a court finds the institution did not provisionally recredit within the ten-day period and either "did not make a good faith investigation" of the alleged error or "did not have a reasonable basis for believing that the consumer's account was not in error."

Where the facts are contested, the two regimes touch. If the claim is that a fraudster used a captured passcode, the FAQ answers put that inside the definition and the liability tiers at 1005.6 apply. Those tiers, and the 60-day statement deadline governing all of them, are worked through in [The 60-Day Line Where Debit Card Fraud Stops Being Capped](/2026/09/14/the-60-day-line-where-debit-card-fraud-stops-being-capped/). Section 1005.6(b)(4) also requires an institution to extend the deadlines to "a reasonable period" where the delay "was due to extenuating circumstances," which is the provision that matters when a hospital stay sits between the statement and the discovery.

## Instruments that carry their own protection

The protection is in the instrument, and it is chosen before the money moves. A credit card carries two separate rights. [12 CFR 1026.12(b)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/12/) caps liability for unauthorized use at "the lesser of $50 or the amount of money, property, labor, or services obtained by the unauthorized use before notification to the card issuer." Independently, [12 CFR 1026.13](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/13/) defines a billing error to include an extension of credit "for property or services not accepted by the consumer or the consumer's designee, or not delivered to the consumer or the consumer's designee as agreed." Goods paid for and never shipped are a billing error on a credit card, and nothing comparable exists for a completed push payment out of a deposit account. Notice must be in writing and reach the creditor "no later than 60 days after the creditor transmitted the first periodic statement that reflects the alleged billing error," and the creditor must resolve it within two complete billing cycles, "in no event later than 90 days."

Section 1026.12(c) adds a third right with fine print. A cardholder who has tried in good faith to resolve a dispute with the merchant "may assert against the card issuer all claims (other than tort claims) and defenses arising out of the transaction," but only where the amount "exceeds $50," and the transaction occurred in the cardholder's own state or "within 100 miles from that address." Those limits fall away where the merchant is the card issuer or is controlled by it.

A debit card sits under Regulation E's tiers, weaker than a credit card and stronger than a wire, because an unauthorized debit card transaction falls inside 1005.2(m) while a wire is outside Regulation E altogether. Checks sit outside coverage too, under 1005.3(c)(1), which leaves a forged or altered check to a separate body of state law.

Ordered by what happens when the counterparty turns out to be a stranger who lied, the sequence runs credit card, debit card, ACH, wire, then cash and its equivalents. A request to move money by a method at the far end of that list, from someone who called first, is the tell.

Verification runs in the other direction too, for money arriving rather than leaving. A deposit that posts is not a deposit that is final, and the gap between the two is the mechanism behind overpayment scams, which is why [Why Your Deposit Is Not Available Yet: Funds Availability Rules](/2026/09/05/why-your-deposit-is-not-available-yet-funds-availability-rules/) is worth reading before refunding anyone a difference.

## Common questions

**The caller's number matched the bank's exactly. Does spoofing change the analysis?** Not under 1005.2(m), which turns on who initiated the transfer. Spoofed caller ID goes to how convincing the deception was, not to who entered the payment instruction. It matters for the criminal complaint: the number belongs in the IC3 filing with any text messages, which the FinCEN fact sheet lists among the secondary information useful for tracing.

**Is a wire really final as a matter of law, or is that the bank's policy?** Closer to law than policy. UCC 4A-211(c) provides that after a payment order has been accepted, "cancellation or amendment of the order is not effective unless the receiving bank agrees." The OCC's consumer site describes wires as "intended to be a final and irrevocable method of payment." A sending bank can request a recall; it cannot compel one.

**Does filing with several agencies improve the odds?** They are not interchangeable. The complaint at ic3.gov is the one connected to the Recovery Asset Team and, through it, to the FinCEN program for funds sent abroad, and the fact sheet is explicit that victims should not contact FinCEN directly. A CFPB complaint produces a written company response on a 15-day clock; an FTC report feeds enforcement data. The IC3 complaint, with complete account numbers on both sides, is the one under time pressure.

**A scammer got a one-time passcode and moved the money. Is that also outside the rule?** No, and the distinction is the whole point. FAQ Question 5 treats a third party who tricks a consumer into providing a "texted account confirmation code" and then initiates the transfer as having made an unauthorized transfer, and Question 6 confirms the consumer has not "furnished an access device" by being deceived. That claim runs through 1005.11 error resolution and the 1005.6 liability tiers.

**The bank denied the claim over the phone. Is anything owed in writing?** If a notice of error was given, yes. Section 1005.11(d)(1) requires a written explanation of the findings and notice of the right to request the documents the institution relied on. A request for documentation or "additional information or clarification concerning an electronic fund transfer" is itself an error under 1005.11(a)(1)(vii), so asking in writing starts the clock even where the underlying transfer is not covered.

The rule was written in the 1970s around a straightforward question about a card and a terminal: did the account holder do this, or did someone else. A payment instruction a stranger can talk a person into issuing from a phone in a parking lot answers that question cleanly, in the direction that ends the claim. The branch manager on Wednesday morning was reading the definition correctly.

title: The EE Bond Guarantee: How a Low Stated Rate Still Doubles
description: Treasury guarantees a Series EE bond reaches twice its purchase price at 20 years. That works out to about 3.53% compounded, payable only to a holder who reaches month 240.
content:
The [TreasuryDirect page for Series EE savings bonds](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/savings-bonds/ee-bonds/) shows one number: 2.40%, "For EE bonds issued May 1, 2026 to October 31, 2026." That holds its own against the [FDIC](https://www.fdic.gov/national-rates-and-rate-caps) national average of 1.71% for a 12-month CD as of August 17, 2026. Next to what a competitive online bank pays on a one-year certificate, it reads as a rate nobody would lock money away for two decades to get.

The stated rate is not the offer. Directly above that rate box on the same Treasury page sits the sentence carrying the actual terms: "For EE bonds you buy now, we guarantee that the bond will double in value in 20 years, even if we have to add money at 20 years to make that happen." The rule behind it is in the offering itself, at [31 CFR 351.35(f)(2)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-351): "At original maturity, the redemption value of a book-entry bond shall not be less than double the purchase price of the bond." Original maturity, under [31 CFR 351.34(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-351), is "20 years after the issue date."

Doubling over twenty years is a compound rate whether or not anyone prints it. Two to the power of one-twentieth is 1.035265, so the guarantee is worth about 3.53% a year compounded annually. At the stated 2.40%, compounded semiannually as the regulation requires, $10,000 grows to $16,114.64 in twenty years. The guarantee has to supply the other $3,885.36, and it supplies it in a single entry on a single day.

Three things follow. The return is not a curve but a step: a holder earns 2.40% at every point from month twelve through month 239, then 3.53% at month 240, with nothing in between. Leaving early costs little in dollars and a lot in opportunity, the reverse of how a certificate of deposit behaves. And a CD ladder run over the same twenty years is not a contest between 3.53% and whatever a five-year CD pays today, because one side is fixed for the whole period, the other resets four times, and the tax code treats the two in opposite ways.

## Two rates on the same bond

The stated rate is set twice a year and then frozen. [31 CFR 351.35(c)(1)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-351) puts the schedule in writing: "The Secretary or the Secretary's designee will furnish a fixed rate of interest in announcements published each May 1 and November 1." Paragraph (b)(1) fixes what that announcement buys: a rate "established for the life of the bond, including the extended maturity period, unless, prior to the beginning of such maturity period, the Secretary either announces a different fixed rate applicable to the extended maturity period, or we expressly amend the terms and conditions applicable to the extended maturity period."

Accrual is monthly, compounding semiannual. Paragraph (d): "Interest accrues on the first day of each month; that is, we add the interest earned on a bond during any given month to its value at the beginning of the following month. The accrued interest compounds semiannually." Semiannual compounding at a 2.40% nominal rate produces an annual percentage yield of 2.414%, which is the rate at which the bond accrues in every month short of the twentieth anniversary, before the early-redemption penalty set out below.

What the guarantee is worth, if the bond survives to month 240, comes out of the two numbers in the regulation, double and twenty years, and does not move when the stated rate moves:

| Fixed rate at issue | $10,000 grown at that rate for 20 years | What the guarantee must add | Share of the final $20,000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.10% | $10,201.96 | $9,798.04 | 48.99% |
| 2.10% | $15,186.33 | $4,813.67 | 24.07% |
| 2.40% | $16,114.64 | $3,885.36 | 19.43% |
| 2.70% | $17,098.19 | $2,901.81 | 14.51% |

The first row is not hypothetical. The rate table on Treasury's page for [EE bonds issued May 2005 and later](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/savings-bonds/ee-bonds/may-2005-and-later/) shows 0.10% for every announcement from November 2015 through May 2022, and nothing above 0.60% in any announcement going back to May 2012. Bonds bought in that stretch carry a stated rate that rounds to nothing and a guarantee that will eventually deliver close to half their redemption value in one payment. The bond issued in May 2022 reaches its twentieth anniversary in May 2042; nothing before then reflects the promise.

A bond needs a shade under 3.50% nominal, compounded semiannually, to reach twice its purchase price without help. Three announcements since May 2005 have cleared that line: 3.50% in May 2005, 3.70% in May 2006, and 3.60% in November 2006. Every announcement from May 2007 onward has come in below it, so for nineteen years the doubling clause has been the operative term rather than a backstop that occasionally matters.

## Month 240, and the month before it

No bank product behaves the way this step function does. Put $10,000 into an EE bond issued this month and the redemption value moves like this:

| Held for | Redemption value at 2.40% | Annualized |
|---|---|---|
| 1 year | $10,241.44 | 2.414% |
| 5 years | $11,266.92 | 2.414% |
| 10 years | $12,694.34 | 2.414% |
| 15 years | $14,302.61 | 2.414% |
| 19 years | $15,734.74 | 2.414% |
| 19 years, 11 months | $16,082.63 | 2.414% |
| 20 years | $20,000.00 | 3.5265% |

Look at the second-to-last row. Redeem one month early and the payment is $16,082.63; wait, and it is $20,000. That one month carries $3,917.37 on a $10,000 purchase — close to two-thirds of the $6,082.63 the bond accumulated across the preceding 239 months put together.

The adjustment is described on Treasury's own page as conditional and retrospective: "If you keep the bond for 20 years, we will make a one-time adjustment, if necessary, to fulfill this guarantee." The same page sends holders to their TreasuryDirect account or the Savings Bond Calculator for a bond's current value, and the only caveat it attaches to those figures is the one for bonds under five years old. Nothing in the wording makes the adjustment part of what accrues month by month.

Timing inside a month is a smaller matter but runs the same way. Because interest accrues on the first day of each month under 351.35(d), the redemption value is flat from the second of the month to the last day of it. Redeeming on the 3rd and redeeming on the 28th produce the same figure; waiting until the 1st adds a month. Bonds under five years old carry a further display quirk, flagged on the Treasury page: "For bonds less than 5 years old, values shown in TreasuryDirect and the Calculator don't include the last three months of interest."

Redemption at twenty years is also a decision someone has to make. Electronic bonds are redeemed automatically at final maturity, which [31 CFR 351.34(b)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-351) places at "30 years after the issue date," not at twenty. A bond left alone past the twentieth anniversary keeps running under whatever terms apply to its last decade.

## Twelve months locked, three months forfeited

The exit rules are short. [31 CFR 351.6(b)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-351): "Bonds with issue dates on or after February 1, 2003. You may redeem your Series EE savings bond at any time beginning twelve months after its issue date." There is no fee schedule that shortens this and no partial exit, because the bond is not redeemable at all inside the first year.

After twelve months, paragraph (e) of 351.35 governs: "If you redeem a bond with an issue date of May 1, 2005, or thereafter, less than five years following the issue date, we reduce the overall earning period from the issue date by three months. However, the redemption value of a bond subject to the 3-month interest penalty shall not be reduced below the issue price. This penalty does not apply to bonds redeemed 5 years or more after the issue date."

Three months of interest at 2.40% is not much money:

| Redeemed at | Value without penalty | Value after penalty | Forfeited |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 months | $10,241.44 | $10,180.54 | $60.90 |
| 24 months | $10,488.71 | $10,426.34 | $62.37 |
| 36 months | $10,741.95 | $10,678.07 | $63.88 |
| 59 months | $11,244.54 | $11,177.67 | $66.87 |

Sixty-one dollars on $10,000 buys the whole first-year exit. The second sentence of paragraph (e) marks the structural difference from a bank certificate: the penalty cannot push the redemption value below what was paid. A CD penalty has no such floor. Under [12 CFR 1030.4(b)(6)(ii)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1030/4/) a bank states "how it is calculated," and when that calculation is a year of interest on a CD three months old, the shortfall comes out of the deposit, which is worked through in [CD Early Withdrawal Penalties: The Disclosure and the Deduction](/2026/09/22/cd-early-withdrawal-penalties-the-disclosure-and-the-deduction/).

One more asymmetry sits in [31 CFR 351.7](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-351), a single sentence: "The Secretary of the Treasury may not call Series EE bonds for redemption prior to final maturity." The twenty-year clock cannot be cut short from the other side. A long CD carrying a call provision can be, and the call arrives precisely when the rate has become valuable, the mechanism described in [Callable CDs: The Risk That Only Appears When Rates Fall](/2026/08/29/callable-cds-the-risk-that-only-appears-when-rates-fall/).

Series I bonds run on the same twelve-month lock and the same three-month forfeiture, with a rate that moves instead of a doubling clause; the comparison is in [I Bonds vs a High-Yield Savings Account: The 12-Month Lock](/2026/09/24/i-bonds-vs-a-high-yield-savings-account-the-12-month-lock/).

## A CD ladder run over the same twenty years

Twenty years in five-year rungs means four maturities and four reinvestments at rates nobody knows yet. That is the comparison, and pretending the first rung's rate holds for the whole period is where the arithmetic usually goes wrong.

Today's averages give a sense of the floor. FDIC national rates as of August 17, 2026 were 1.36% at 60 months, 1.34% at 36 months and 1.71% at 12 months, with savings accounts at 0.38%. Compounded annually for twenty years, 1.36% turns $10,000 into $13,101.83 and never comes near doubling. Nobody builds a ladder at the national average, but it shows what the curve looks like when the long end is not being paid for; a ladder locking twenty years of five-year rungs at those levels would lose to the guarantee. The mechanics of building one are in [Building a CD Ladder When 12-Month CDs Pay the Most](/2026/08/19/building-a-cd-ladder-when-12-month-cds-pay-the-most/).

Take a more generous assumption instead: a ladder that averages 4% across all twenty years, reinvestment risk waved away. Pre-tax, $10,000 at 4% compounds to $21,911.23, and passes $20,000 after about 17.7 years. On rate alone the ladder wins, and it wins early.

Tax moves the line, because the two instruments are taxed on opposite schedules. CD interest is taxable in the year it is credited even when it cannot be withdrawn, which is the subject of [Why You Owe Tax on a 5-Year CD You Cannot Touch Yet](/2026/09/25/why-you-owe-tax-on-a-5-year-cd-you-cannot-touch-yet/). EE bond interest can be deferred to redemption, and is exempt from state and local income tax in every year. Paying the CD's tax out of the CD's own interest lowers its compounding rate for two decades; the EE pays once, at the end, on the full gain:

| Marginal rate assumed | Ladder at 4%, taxed each year | EE bond, $20,000 taxed once | CD rate needed to match |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12% federal, no state tax | $19,974.93 | $18,800.00 | 3.64% |
| 22% federal, no state tax | $18,486.64 | $17,800.00 | 3.75% |
| 22% federal + 5% state | $17,782.61 | $17,800.00 | 4.01% |
| 24% federal + 5% state | $17,508.19 | $17,600.00 | 4.04% |

Read the last column. It gives the average gross rate a twenty-year ladder has to hit, every rung, to end up where the guarantee ends up. In a state with no income tax and a low federal bracket the hurdle is 3.64%. Add a state income tax and a middle bracket and it crosses 4%, which is above the 3.53% the guarantee implies, because deferral and the state exemption are each worth something on their own.

Two cautions on that table. The $10,000 of EE interest arrives in one tax year and can push a return into a higher bracket than the one assumed, a risk the ladder spreads out by construction. And the whole comparison assumes the ladder actually averages 4%; four resets over twenty years is four chances for it not to.

Put an amount and a set of rungs in below to see when each one frees up.

{% include tools/ladder-builder.html %}

## The tax treatment, in both directions

Treasury's summary is three lines: "Federal income tax: Yes. State and local income tax: No. Federal estate, gift, and excise taxes; state estate or inheritance taxes: Yes." The state exemption is the same feature that distinguishes Treasury bills from certificates, and it scales with the state rate rather than with the size of the deposit, as set out in [Treasury Bills vs CDs: The Tax Break That Changes the Comparison](/2026/09/23/treasury-bills-vs-cds-the-tax-break-that-changes-the-comparison/). At a 5% state rate, 3.5265% free of state tax is equivalent to about 3.71% that is not.

Federal timing is a choice, made once and applied to everything. Treasury states it as two options: "put off (defer) reporting the interest until you file a federal income tax return for the year in which you actually get the interest, or report the interest each year even though you don't actually get the interest then." Switching from deferral to annual reporting requires no permission but is not selective: "you must do this for all the savings bonds for the Social Security Number whose tax return this is," including all interest earned in earlier years. Switching the other way requires Form 3115 or the procedure in IRS Publication 550.

Treasury flags one situation for annual reporting: a bond in a child's name, where "The child may be paying taxes at a lower rate than will be true years later when the bond matures." Who owes the tax is settled separately, by the registration rather than by who paid. Treasury's own table is blunt about it: if "You buy the bond but someone else is named as the only owner (for example, your child)," the tax falls on "The person who is named as the owner (not you)." What a child's own rate turns out to be has its own rules, covered in [Savings Accounts for Kids: Custodial Rules and the Kiddie Tax](/2026/09/17/savings-accounts-for-kids-custodial-rules-and-the-kiddie-tax/).

The education exclusion is a separate track with its own form. [31 CFR 351.81](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-351) points to it, and the mechanics are on [Form 8815](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f8815.pdf), "Exclusion of Interest From Series EE and I U.S. Savings Bonds Issued After 1989 (For Filers With Qualified Higher Education Expenses)." The 2025 form asks for "the total proceeds (principal and interest) from all series EE and I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989 that you cashed during 2025" on line 5, then rations the exclusion by income. The note above line 10 is where most filers stop: "If line 9 is $114,500 or more if single, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse; or $179,250 or more if married filing jointly, stop. You cannot take the exclusion." The phase-out begins at $99,500 and $149,250 respectively, across a $15,000 band for single filers and a $30,000 band for joint filers. The surviving amount goes on Schedule B (Form 1040), line 3.

The timing is where this turns awkward. Line 9 of Form 8815 asks for "your modified adjusted gross income" in the year the bonds were cashed, not in the year they were bought, and a bond bought to reach its doubling date is cashed two decades after anyone could have known what that income would be. How taxed interest compounds against inflation over a period that long is a separate calculation, laid out in [The Tax Bite on Savings Interest: What Your Real Yield Is](/2026/08/26/the-tax-bite-on-savings-interest-what-your-real-yield-is/).

## The ceiling the strategy runs into

The guarantee is attractive per dollar and capped in dollars. [31 CFR 363.52(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-363): "The principal amount of book-entry savings bonds that you may acquire in any calendar year is limited to $10,000 for Series EE savings bonds and $10,000 for Series I savings bonds." Treasury's own page repeats it in plainer terms: "The limit applies to the Social Security Number of the first person named on the bond." One carve-out sits on the limits page: "If you have an individual account and an entity account in TreasuryDirect that use the same Social Security Number, you can purchase up to the limits in each of the 2 accounts."

Gifts do not route around it. Paragraph (b) of the same section counts a gift "for the account of the recipient for the year in which the bonds are delivered to the recipient," and Treasury adds that a bond sitting undelivered is "in a special 'gift box'" belonging to nobody's limit yet. Co-ownership does not multiply it either: "only the bonds for which you are the first named owner count toward your limit."

The floors and increments are small. [31 CFR 363.53](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-363) sets a $25 minimum purchase "with additional one-cent increments above that amount." [31 CFR 363.57](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-363) applies the same $25 minimum to redemptions and adds the important clause: "Redemptions will be comprised of principal and proportionate interest." Partial redemption of an electronic bond is allowed, subject to [31 CFR 363.54](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-363), which requires "a redemption value of at least $25" to remain. Treasury's plain-language version adds what the proportionality means in practice: "If you cash only part of what a bond is worth, you only get the interest on the part you cash." A paper bond has no such option and "must be cashed for its entire value."

One restriction has no bank equivalent. [31 CFR 363.58](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-363): "Bonds may not be pledged or used as collateral for the performance of an obligation." A certificate of deposit can secure a loan, which is often the reason a saver tolerates a penalty clause. An EE bond cannot, so the twenty-year commitment is not softened by borrowing against it.

## What the twentieth anniversary opens

The guarantee resolves at twenty years and a second set of terms begins. Treasury states the reservation: "For bonds bought since May 2005, we may change the interest rate or the way the EE bond earns interest for the last 10 years of the bond's 30-year life. If we do that, we must do it before the bond is 20 years old."

The same authority is written into 351.35(b)(1), which fixes the rate for the life of the bond "unless, prior to the beginning of such maturity period, the Secretary either announces a different fixed rate applicable to the extended maturity period, or we expressly amend the terms and conditions applicable to the extended maturity period." The notice comes before the extension, not during it, so the terms for the final decade are knowable by the anniversary.

Treasury spells out the consequence: "If you do not want that new interest rate or the new way the bond will earn interest in its last 10 years, you can cash it when it reaches 20 years and has at least doubled what you paid for it." The decision is a live one, and the guarantee has already paid by the time it arrives. Whatever rate applies to years twenty-one through thirty applies to a balance twice the size of the original purchase.

Interest stops at the end. Under 351.34(b) bonds "cease to earn interest at final maturity," thirty years from issue. A bond held past that date earns nothing at all while remaining fully redeemable, which is the quiet cost of forgetting one exists. Treasury used to run a lookup for exactly that situation; its [Treasury Hunt page](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/savings-bonds/treasury-hunt/) now reads "As of September 30, 2025, the Treasury Hunt® tool is no longer available" and points anyone who suspects they hold an unredeemed lost, stolen, or destroyed bond to the savings bond forms page to submit a claim. That is a different problem from a bank balance going dormant and escheating to a state, described in [How a Savings Account Goes Dormant and Ends Up With the State](/2026/09/04/how-a-savings-account-goes-dormant-and-ends-up-with-the-state/).

## What the guarantee is measured against

A twenty-year commitment invites a twenty-year comparison, and Treasury publishes one on itself. The [daily par yield curve](https://home.treasury.gov/resource-center/data-chart-center/interest-rates/TextView?type=daily_treasury_yield_curve) put the 20-year Treasury at 5.38% on September 18, 2026, with the 5-year at 4.86%. Both are exempt from state and local income tax on the same footing as a savings bond. Against those numbers the EE bond's implied 3.53% is not a high long rate, and the guarantee is not a claim to be one.

The guarantee is a floor on a nominal dollar figure, known in advance, with no price risk attached. A marketable twenty-year Treasury can be sold before maturity at whatever the market pays that day, which may be well under face value. An EE bond has one price, published in the account, and that price never falls. The trade is liquidity and market upside for certainty about a single number twenty years out.

That certainty is nominal. Doubling over twenty years preserves purchasing power only if prices rise less than about 3.5% a year over the same period, and the EE structure contains nothing that responds to inflation. A Series I bond runs the other way: its rate adjusts, and no doubling guarantee exists.

What settles whether the structure fits is not a rate question. It is the issue month, since the anniversary is a date and not a range; whether the money can sit untouched until that date, because an exit before it leaves the stated rate as the entire return and forfeits the clause; and the $10,000 cap per Social Security Number per year, which decides whether the guarantee covers a meaningful share of a portfolio or a corner of one.

## Common questions

**Is the doubling a rate or a lump sum?** Mechanically it is a lump sum. The bond earns its stated rate month by month, and at original maturity Treasury makes what its own page calls "a one-time adjustment, if necessary" so that the redemption value is at least twice the purchase price. Expressed as a compound rate over the full twenty years it comes to about 3.53%, but no part of it accrues before the anniversary.

**What happens if the bond is redeemed at nineteen years?** It pays the stated rate and nothing else. On a $10,000 bond issued at 2.40%, nineteen years produces $15,734.74; the twentieth year produces $20,000. The guarantee has no partial version and does not scale with time held.

**Can an EE bond be worth less than what was paid for it?** No. [31 CFR 351.35(e)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/part-351) states that "the redemption value of a bond subject to the 3-month interest penalty shall not be reduced below the issue price," and the penalty is the only deduction the bond carries. A CD penalty has no equivalent floor.

**Does the $10,000 limit apply to the purchase price or the redemption value?** To the purchase. 31 CFR 363.52(a) caps "the principal amount of book-entry savings bonds that you may acquire in any calendar year." What the bonds grow to is not counted against any later year's limit.

**Can the interest be reported annually instead of at redemption?** Yes, without IRS permission, but the election covers every savings bond held under that Social Security Number and requires reporting all prior years' accrued interest in the year of the change. Reversing it takes Form 3115 or the procedure in Publication 550. Which method suits a particular return is a question for a tax professional.

An EE bond bought today turns on a calendar date, not a rate. The 2.40% on the purchase screen is what a holder earns for being early; the number that matters is printed in a regulation, applies once, and applies only to whoever still holds the bond on the twentieth anniversary of its issue month.
